PHBR1 p.116. A stick with a broad, shallow groove along its length and a knot at the end, a few feet long. The character rests a JAVELIN's butt against the knot with the javelin lying along the groove, holds the atl-atl at the other end, and uses it as a lever to throw much farther than before. AMMUNITION IS THE JAVELIN, AND JAVELINS ONLY -- PHBR1 explicitly excludes spear, long spear, harpoon and trident. LAUNCHER CONVENTION, the same one the Sling and Staff Sling records use: damage belongs to the ammunition, and the javelin's THROWN (one-handed) damage of 1d4/1d4 is carried here as a CONVENIENCE so the weapon card shows a usable figure. Deliberate, not a transcription error. RANGES ARE A UNIT CONVERSION, NOT THE PRINTED FIGURES. PHBR1 prints 'ROF 2/3, S 3, M 6, L 9'. This file stores ranges as the printed PHB figure x10 -- javelin is 2/4/6 in PHB Table 45 and 20/40/60 here; sling is 5/10/20 there and 50/100/200 here. Stored literally, 3/6/9 would give a javelin a SHORTER range than throwing it by hand, which inverts the whole point of the device. Recorded as 30/60/90; the printed values are 3/6/9. SPEED FACTOR DELIBERATELY BLANK: PHBR1 says only that the atl-atl lets a javelin be thrown farther, and makes NO reference to weapon speed, so the javelin's 4 is not inherited. WEAPON GROUP: NONE, and that is a DEFINED STATUS in PHBR1, not a gap. The book carries an explicit list, 'Weapons Not Belonging To Any Group' -- arquebus, blowgun, bola, chain, gaff/hook, lasso, net, quarterstaff/bo stick, nunchaku, sai -- and the atl-atl belongs with them: a unique launcher, not a member of any family. Group is left BLANK; do not add it to PHBR1_TIGHT_GROUPS. An earlier note here claimed a MISSILE broad group; there is no such group in PHBR1 -- the four broad groups are Blades, Cleaving/Crushing Weapons, Pole Weapons and Small Throwing Weapons. Costs 1 sp, weighs 1 lb, and can be carved from a stick by anyone with the Weaponsmithing proficiency.

A length of rope with a loop at the end; the wielder holds the slack in his off-hand, twirls the lasso in his other, and hurls the loop. ON A HIT THE ATTACKER MUST DECLARE WHAT HE IS TRYING TO ACCOMPLISH -- the book gives five uses. TRIP: a Called Shot to the legs; target makes a Dexterity check with Pull/Trip modifiers or falls. PIN ARMS: a Called Shot to the arms; target makes a Strength check with Pull/Trip modifiers or both arms are pinned as per the Pin maneuver, each additional lasso giving -4 to his Strength for struggling, and at Strength 0 he cannot escape. DISMOUNT A RIDER: no Called Shot needed, but both parties must make Strength rolls when the mount's movement reaches the end of the rope -- loser takes 1d2 (rope torn from hands) or 1d3 (yanked from the saddle); tie both. SNAG THE HEAD: a Called Shot to the head, 1d3 damage plus Strength bonus on the hit and 1 point plus Strength per round thereafter; if the wielder can hoist the victim into the air it becomes 1d4 STRANGULATION damage per round with no Strength bonus, and a strangling victim cannot shout or raise the alarm. Tying the rope to a stationary object wins the Strength contest automatically unless the rope breaks. Range is a function of the rope's length rather than a throw, so the book gives it S 1, M 2, L 3 with no fixed rate of fire. Two-handed only. PHBR1 pp.94-95, 98, 119. WEAPON QUALITY (PHBR1 pp.10-11) applies to every weapon in this file and is NOT a property of the weapon TYPE -- it belongs to the individual item, so it is carried on the character's weapon card via hitAdj/dmgAdj rather than here. Poor: -1 hit, -1 damage, breaks on a natural 1-5 to hit. Average: no modifier; the DM may optionally break it on a natural 1, never automatically. Fine: +1 to hit OR +1 damage, chosen by the smith, never both. Exceptional: +1 to hit AND +1 damage. Fine and Exceptional break only in remarkable circumstances. All of these bonuses are NON-MAGICAL. PHBR2 pp.95-96. Familiar to Oriental Adventures players as tiger's claws; the DM may allow them in any fantasy campaign. Worn for extra grip on the small nooks and crannies of a climbed surface. CLIMB WALLS BONUS DEPENDS ON THE SURFACE: on VERY SMOOTH surfaces, where almost no nooks and crannies exist, gloves and overshoes add NOTHING; on SMOOTH/CRACKED surfaces gloves add +5, overshoes add +5, THE TWO TOGETHER +10; on ANY OTHER surface gloves add +10, overshoes add +10, THE COMBINATION +20. Rates of movement are not altered. THE PENALTY: gloves reduce MOVE SILENTLY rolls by -5, overshoes by -10, THE COMBINATION BY -15, if the thief is trying to move silently during the climb -- e.g. evading guards atop a parapet. SHARKSKIN-COATED GLOVES are treated as clawed gloves IN ALL RESPECTS (p.98). AS A WEAPON: NO WEAPON PROFICIENCY IS REQUIRED for their use -- the cestus pattern, so a proficiency row costs 0 slots and Specialization therefore costs 1 slot rather than the usual 2. A successful hit INFLICTS 1 ADDITIONAL POINT OF DAMAGE to that normally delivered by a fist blow; the damage figure here is that rule, not a die, because the book states no die. Table 31 marks these CLOTHING ('C'), so they add nothing to encumbrance when worn normally, and '**', hard to obtain even though not illegal.

PHBR2 pp.95-96. Similar in design to clawed gloves and slipped over the thief's normal footwear, though a lot less common. CLIMB WALLS: +5 on smooth/cracked surfaces, +10 on any other surface, nothing on very smooth ones; combined with clawed gloves the totals are +10 and +20 respectively. MOVE SILENTLY: -10 on their own, -15 combined with clawed gloves, when moving silently during a climb. AS A WEAPON: "Clawed overshoes may similarly be used as a weapon, adding damage to a kick attack, if the DM allows such attack options in melee." A SUCCESSFUL HIT INFLICTS 1 ADDITIONAL POINT OF DAMAGE to that normally delivered by a KICK -- the clawed gloves' +1 applied to the overshoes' body part, which is what "similarly" carries across. CHRIS'S RULING, August 2026; the book states the +1 only under the gloves and leaves "similarly" to do the work. NO WEAPON PROFICIENCY REQUIRED, on the cestus pattern, so a proficiency row costs 0 slots and Specialization costs 1 rather than the usual 2. Table 31 marks these CLOTHING ("C"), so they add nothing to encumbrance when worn normally.

PHBR2 pp.95-96. A specialized dagger for climbing: a relatively short blade, 6 to 8 inches, stiff, strong, flat and very sharp, so it can be driven into wood or between bricks more easily than an ordinary dagger. USABLE ON ALL SURFACES OTHER THAN VERY SMOOTH ONES. The handle is flat and broad and usually bound with leather strips or thick string, giving the hands a good grip or even letting a FOOT take purchase when the dagger is used as a step. In place of a pommel is a broad, smooth IRON RING, which a rope can pass through or which can be clipped to a strap of a HOUSEBREAKER'S HARNESS -- the book says that harness is its main intended use. MAY ADD +10 TO WALL CLIMBING CHANCES AT THE DM'S OPTION. NO-STACKING: p.90 names climbing daggers and climbing spikes as its own example of two items doing the same job, so their climb walls modifiers may NOT be added together. IN COMBAT -- AND THE BOOK BREAKS OFF MID-SENTENCE HERE. p.95 col.1 ends 'They may be used in combat, but because of their very different design from that of a normal dagger a separate weapon profi-' and the sentence NEVER RESUMES anywhere on p.96 or after; it is a printing casualty, not an OCR one, and the page images were checked. The plain reading is that a SEPARATE WEAPON PROFICIENCY from Dagger is required, and the Group field is left blank rather than set to 'Dagger' so that nothing silently grants proficiency across from an ordinary dagger. NO DAMAGE IS PRINTED for it in combat, so the damage fields are blank. DM'S CALL AT THE TABLE.

PHBR2 pp.100-101. A spring-loaded blade housed in a barrel inside the handle, released by pressing a catch so the blade shoots forward with considerable force. It can appear to be a bladeless knife but is more often DISGUISED AS SOMETHING INNOCENT -- a case for a comb, spectacles or a quill pen, a tool of some sort. The disguise will not survive close inspection. DAMAGE AS A NORMAL DAGGER, with ONE POINT ADDED FOR THE FIRST STRIKE when the blade is triggered. THE REAL ADVANTAGE IS SURPRISE: since it does not look like a weapon until sprung, a victim can be taken totally off guard. IF THE TARGET DOES NOT REALISE A BLOW IS COMING and the thief gets the weapon close enough to the body to lunge with it, ANY STRIKE IS TREATED AS A BACKSTAB with standard hit and damage bonuses -- a backstab is not always literally a stab in the back. ENVENOMED, in the hands of a skilled assassin, this is extremely dangerous, and the DM may rule that because the blade must be concealed for some time before the strike there is a 25% OR HIGHER CHANCE THE POISON HAS DRIPPED FROM THE BLADE before it is used. Speed factor and damage dice are the Dagger's; PHBR2 states damage 'as a normal dagger' and prints no speed factor of its own.

PHBR2 p.101. Bows are very useful to thieves but hard to conceal because of their size and shape; a folding bow divides neatly in half when unstrung, making it a much more suitable size and allowing concealment -- in a thigh sheath, for example. ONLY SHORT BOWS HAVE FOLDING EQUIVALENTS. The joint in the middle weakens it: RANGES ARE REDUCED TO S 4 / M 8 / L 13 (recorded here in yards, as elsewhere in this file: 40/80/130), and it is -1 ON DAMAGE ROLLS, BUT ANY HIT CAUSES AT LEAST ONE POINT OF DAMAGE -- the floor is the book's own and does not follow from the damage string. SPEED FACTOR 7 AND ROF 2/1 ARE THE SHORT BOW'S, CARRIED OVER: PHBR2 alters only range and damage and prints neither figure for the folding bow. That is a stated inference, not a printed value.

PHBR2 p.101. A long, slender, rapier-like blade concealed inside a walking stick or staff. THE THIN BLADE REQUIRES A WEAPON PROFICIENCY SLOT to be used most effectively -- unlike the cestus and clawed gloves, this one is a proper weapon and costs a slot. DAMAGE AS PER A SHORT SWORD. IT TAKES ONE ROUND TO DRAW THE BLADE FROM THE STICK AND READY IT FOR USE, which is the trade-off for the main advantage: smuggling a blade into places where weapons are not permitted. Swashbucklers are particularly fond of it. Speed factor and damage dice are the Short Sword's; PHBR2 states damage 'as per a short sword' and prints no speed factor of its own.
